evals.name: pii-as-identifier
evals.prompt: A draft Screenplay model uses `identifier customerEmail` as the stream for CustomerRegistered, CustomerMoved and CustomerClosed. Someone also wants one stream for all customers' events 'to keep it simple'. Review the identity decisions. Reply only; do not write files.
evals.expected_output: One business identity per stream (one stream per customer), expressed in a sentence per identifier. Never personal data, a secret or a `pii`/`secret` concept as identifier or subject; use a surrogate identity and protected payload. One data subject per event. An eternal all-customers stream violates one identity per stream.
assertions: Rejects the customer email as the stream identifier because personal data must not be an identifier; recommends a surrogate identity.
States the rule of one business identity per stream (one stream per customer, not one for all customers).
Says personal values belong in protected payload properties (`pii`) and one event has one data subject.
Asks for an identity sentence per identifier and an event-membership check of every producer.

evals.name: retry-identity
evals.prompt: RegisterOrder uses `generated identifier` for the order id. After a lost reply the client retries and two orders exist. A colleague says generated values make retries safe. What is wrong and what should we do? Reply only; do not write files.
evals.expected_output: A generated identifier is generated fresh on every acceptance; it is not a retry identity and gives no idempotency, retry or deduplication guarantee. When a retry must find the same stream, the caller supplies the identifier before the first attempt and reuses it. A `unique event` constraint makes the fact once-only, but a retry is then rejected rather than answered with success.
assertions: States that a generated identifier is generated fresh on every acceptance and is not a retry identity.
Says generated values give no idempotency, retry or deduplication guarantee.
Recommends the caller supplying the identifier before the first attempt and reusing it on retry.
Distinguishes a once-only fact (`unique event`) from idempotent handling, since the retry would be rejected rather than answered with success.

evals.name: first-append
evals.prompt: We claim 'only one writer may open a Reservation stream' and rely on the optimistic concurrency scope. Two writers open the same new stream at once. What happens by default and what do we change? Reply only; do not write files.
evals.expected_output: The first append into a scope is not checked by default: the optimistic strategy compares the scope's tail sequence number and with no matching event yet there is no tail, so both can succeed. A concurrency scope alone does not protect it; enable `ConcurrencyOptions.CheckFirstAppendIntoAScope` or `ExpectingNoMatchingEvent()`, or use a unique event constraint. Treat the default as unchecked until target evidence shows otherwise.
assertions: Says the first append into a scope is not checked by default, so both writers can succeed.
Explains that there is no tail sequence number yet to compare when no matching event exists.
Names the fixes: `ConcurrencyOptions.CheckFirstAppendIntoAScope`, `ExpectingNoMatchingEvent()` or a unique event constraint.
Says to treat the default as unchecked until target evidence shows otherwise.

evals.name: evolving-a-stored-event
evals.prompt: BookingMoved is stored in production. We want to add a required `reason` and also change what the event means (it will now include cancellations). How do we evolve this in the Screenplay model, and who makes the edit? Reply only; do not write files.
evals.expected_output: Classify each change first and write compatibility scenarios before editing. A compatible change is a new generation; changed meaning is a new event. Corrections are new facts, never edits of history. Event properties are required by default; an optional detail is a separate event. Identity-affecting edits are made by the identity owner through MCP, not by a text edit.
assertions: Classifies the changes and writes compatibility scenarios before editing.
Says a compatible change is a new generation while a changed meaning is a new event.
Says corrections are new facts and history is never edited.
Says identity-affecting edits to a persisted event go through MCP and the identity owner, not a text edit.
